chapter: Shows, scripts and the Mosby-era names
title: Los Angeles record companies of the late 1940s and what Spikes missed
summary: Willard raises the Exclusive label and War Perkins; Spikes says he lacked promotion savvy, never gave bands professional copies, and might have become a millionaire.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: And this talk about record business in Los Angeles and your label and it mentions the René brothers--Leon and Otis--and their Exclusive Record Company. And then Joe Liggins was on that, right? For Exclusive.
And then it says, "The most aggressive of the executives is War Perkins...and his...

Well, he got out and hustled. He didn't have no business or nothing. He make a record and then he get in a bu...his car and everything and go all around the South and everything and carry it, you know. We didn't hustle everywhere, that we depend on our reputation. O'course, we were young and new in the business. We didn't know what to do. If I knew what I knew now in the record business, then I'd a been a multi-millionaire by now, you know. See, even the songs we wrote, we'd give...publish them, and then we'd give one to this singer and one to that singer instead of sending them out to all the musicians or giving them to all the musicians or havin' a place where they can all obme and get them, you know, like all these other big publishers--if you got a band, you go down there, and they give you a copy of it for your band--you know, what they call a professional copy. We didn't know nothing about that. And we never...uh...uh...you know, just happened and we didn't know nothing about doing none of that stuff. If you had of, we could be multi-millionaires now 'cause coulda had bigger records than...than Mamie Smith 'cause there was the talent here, and you coulda got 'em for glory, you know?
Perkins had a...his company was called Day Company. Is that right?
I don't know what his company was called.
He was also a disc jockey at some point, wasn't he? Wasn't he the first Negro disc jockey in Los Angeles?
I don't know. Does it say that on there?
It doesn't say that here but that's what...I think that's what Roy Loggins told me, and...
Well, maybe he was. I don't know.
And then, 'Hamptone Records is about to be reorganized...'
Yeah, I think so. It doesn't say, but...
I don't know whether he made any, or whether he made one or I don't know what.
